summary:
Atlas – Sky Viewer is a public-facing web application that makes NASA’s SPHEREx infrared observations accessible through interactive exploration and chronological image playback. Users can enter Right Ascension and declination, select a suggested target, or click the sky map to explore a location and view possible catalog matches.
Atlas retrieves real observations covering the selected region and presents compatible images in date order. A timeline slider, playback controls, and frame-by-frame navigation help users investigate potential changes in position or brightness. Observation dates, wavelengths, and data coverage provide context for what they see.
By transforming astronomical archive files into an approachable visual experience, Atlas addresses the challenge of helping anyone explore how the infrared sky changes over time. It supports astronomy education, public engagement, and visual investigation, while allowing previously downloaded sequences to be replayed without internet access.
details:
Atlas connects a familiar map-based experience with real astronomical observations, helping users move from curiosity about the sky to exploring its changes over time.

The application has two main views:

  • Sky view: An interactive SPHEREx infrared sky map with panning, zooming, coordinate entry, and suggested destinations. Clicking a position opens an anchored popup containing coordinates, possible SIMBAD catalog matches, and available object properties.
  • Observation playback: A chronological sequence of images covering the selected coordinates. Users can play or pause, change playback speed, move between individual observations, or scrub backward and forward using the timeline. Saved observations are grouped by object, with available wavelength choices inside each entry.

The Python backend searches NASA/IPAC IRSA using Simple Image Access, with Table Access Protocol as a fallback. It retrieves individual FITS image cutouts, reads their observation times and spectral information, and prepares browser-friendly images. The sky map uses an all-sky mosaic; the playback uses separate, dated observations.

For more consistent comparisons, Atlas selects observations with closely matched wavelengths, aligns images to a common sky coordinate grid, and applies a shared brightness stretch. Available measurements remain visible, while genuinely missing image cells appear as a checkerboard. Observation details distinguish available coverage from pixels meeting stricter quality criteria.

Downloaded FITS files, rendered images, and JSON metadata are stored locally without a database. A resumable batch downloader prepares preset targets across detector bands, reuses validated downloads, and retries failures. Previously saved sequences support offline playback; retrieving new observations and browsing the full sky map require internet access.

We developed Atlas using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Lucide, and Aladin Lite for the interface, and Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Requests, and Pillow for data retrieval and processing. Automated backend, frontend, and browser checks support validation. The application runs on a standard computer with a web browser.

The project’s creativity comes from combining an immersive infrared sky explorer, contextual object information, and time-based observation playback in one interface. We considered accessibility, mobile layouts, unreliable connections, download delays, scientific transparency, and the distinction between wavelength differences and temporal changes.

Atlas’s intended impact is to make NASA’s archive approachable for students, educators, and curious members of the public. It supports visual investigation of potential motion and variability; confirming a scientific discovery requires further analysis.
